newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian govt plans confidence vote on mini-budget.
newsitem.headline: Italian govt plans confidence vote on mini-budget.

text.p: Italy's centre-left government said on Monday it had decided to call a confidence vote in the lower house of parliament to ram a controversial mini-budget past hundreds of opposition amendments.
It will be the 20th do-or-die confidence vote called by Prime Minister Romano Prodi since he took office a year ago.
Coalition leaders were due to decide later on Monday the wording and timing of the motion. A timetable released last week for the lower house pencilled in a confidence vote for Tuesday.

The 1997 mini-budget is designed to cut 15.5 trillion lire ($9.1 billion) from this year's deficit in a bid to meet tough criteria laid down in the Maastricht Treaty for founder members of the planned European single currency.

The package has been bitterly criticised by the centre-right Freedom Alliance opposition and even by centrists within Prodi's own coalition for demanding early payment of taxes by companies on their severance payment funds.

Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi initially sought six trillion lire from the anticipated taxes but agreed to reduce this to five trillion in the wake of widespread discontent and make up the difference with the help of tax amnesties.
However the cut was not enough for many parliamentarians and the budget committee rejected the proposed mini-budget last month after two centre-left deputies broke government ranks.

The hard-left Communist Refoundation, which secures Prodi's majority in the lower house, voted with the government and budget rebels in the committee indicated they would back the coalition if the budget was put to a confidence test.
The full lower house of parliament started debate on the mini-budget last week but has not yet decided what to do about the severance fund taxation.
The cabinet decided to call a confidence vote at a meeting on Monday, Prodi's office said in a statement. The wording of the motion will indicate what amendments have been accepted.

All other proposed changes will be swept away, allowing the bill to move to the Senate, the upper house, for approval. Under Italian law, the budget must be ratified by both houses of parliament before the end of May or else scrapped.
The Freedom Alliance staged a mass demonstration at the weekend in Milan to protest against the government and its economic record.

Prodi has introduced just under 100 trillion lire of belt-tightening measures over the past year as he fights to lower the budget deficit to three percent of Gross Domestic Product, as demanded by the Maastricht Treaty for aspirants to the single currency, the euro.
The deficit/GDP ratio was 6.7 percent in 1996 and Prodi defended his policies on Monday in an interview with La Repubblica newspaper.
"With public accounts out of control it is useless pretending that we don't have to take serious measures," Prodi said. "The medicine is bitter but it is good," he added.
"We wanted 18 months of sacrifices and then the country will pick up. I'm already seeing signs of this," Prodi was quoted as saying.
